title: Stop Chasing Results
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: This piece from The Mindful Manager challenges the performance-management orthodoxy that treats KPIs and outcomes as the primary language of organisational success. Using a personal anecdote about wedding-dress weight-loss goals—in which obsessing over the scale did nothing to change the number—the author draws a direct analogy to how organisations set revenue targets, retention rates, and productivity dashboards while ignoring the underlying behaviours that generate those results. Applying Goodhart's Law ("when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"), the author argues that judging people solely on numbers produces optimisation of the number rather than the behaviours that produced it—sometimes quietly rewarding shortcuts, aggressive tactics, and corner-cutting. The piece offers practical guidance for leaders: identify the real behavioural ingredients behind success—rapport-building, proactive responsiveness, domain credibility—and recognise those behaviours even when outcomes don't cooperate. Senior leaders aren't wrong to watch outcome metrics; the mistake is treating those targets as the entire conversation rather than as the starting point for harder questions. The article closes with a sharp diagnostic: if someone wanted recognition in your organisation tomorrow, what behaviours would they learn to display—and are those the behaviours you actually want more of?
points: Most organisations commit what the author calls the Measurement Trap: fixating on lagging outcome metrics (KPIs, sales figures, retention rates) while ignoring the leading behavioural indicators—rapport, proactive check-ins, consistent reliability—that actually determine whether those outcomes will repeat.

Goodhart's Law applied to leadership: once employees are judged solely on a number, they optimise the number rather than the behaviours that produced it, potentially rewarding shortcuts or inflated reporting that won't appear in the dashboard until damage is already done.
Performance problems are visible in behaviour long before they appear in a dashboard—making behavioural awareness a faster and more corrective early-warning signal than any KPI review cycle.

Senior leaders default to metric-watching because they can't observe hundreds of daily interactions; the solution isn't to abolish targets but to treat them as starting points that should prompt better questions about why people stay, leave, succeed, or stall.

The most diagnostic question any leader can ask is: 'If someone wanted recognition here tomorrow, what behaviours would they learn to display?'—because the answer reveals whether the reward system actually reinforces the culture the organisation claims to want.
quotes: Most performance problems are visible in behaviour long before they appear in a dashboard. By the time the numbers shift, the habits producing those results are often already firmly established.

Economist Charles Goodhart famously observed that “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”. The moment people are judged solely on a number, they often start optimising the number itself rather than the behaviours that originally produced it.
Ultimately, outcomes tell you whether you succeeded. But it is behaviours that tell you whether you’re likely to succeed again. We should be playing the long game.

More importantly, are you recognising those behaviours when the result wasn’t the one you hoped for? When organisations reward outcomes alone, they risk undervaluing people doing excellent work in difficult circumstances.
Organisations that focus only on performance are essentially measuring history. Organisations that focus on behaviours are shaping the future.

The number wasn’t going to magically change because I stared at it every morning with enough emotional intensity. What I actually needed was habits, structure and consistency. The same applies to organisations.
If someone wanted to earn recognition in your organisation tomorrow, what behaviours would they quickly learn to display? And are those the behaviours you actually want more of?
